note: Open questions seeded with a deploy. Keyed on slug: adding one here adds it to the site, and an answer or an edit made on the site is never overwritten by this file.

questions.title: Where is Broxtowe House — and is there more than one?
questions.detail:
The 1921 census schedule gives Dr Kneebone's postal address as "Broxtow House, The Park, Nottingham" — spelt without the e. No house of that name is in the record, and it is on none of the labels on Dougal de Havilland's map. His household sits in the enumerator's round between 19 Park Terrace and Sunnyside, which is where the record provisionally places the house, at **#406**.

**A second household complicates it.** Mary Enfield, 79, her brother Henry, 71, an artist, her companion and two servants were also returned at Broxtowe House — and their schedule sits in the same continuous round but **between 5 and 7 Park Valley, 230 metres away**. Findmypast indexes them as 6 Park Valley, but the original record says Broxtowe House, and 6 Park Valley is not a candidate: that house is Stuart Cottage, built c1835-45, with a listed description of its own.

So either **two houses in The Park carried the name**, or one of the two households is out of position in the enumerator's book. 20 Park Terrace holds no 1921 record and remains a candidate for the Kneebone end. Is the name still known at either end of the estate? Is it on a gatepost, a deed, a rate book, or an older map?

questions.title: Which hospital did the nine doctors at Broxtowe House serve?
questions.detail: Nine house surgeons and house physicians, aged 26 to 33, living in one Park house in June 1921 with no patients and no family. Nottingham General Hospital at Standard Hill is the obvious answer on geography alone, and the hospital's own history records it taking houses in The Park, Park Terrace and the Ropewalk as doctors' residences — but dates that to 1969. If a hospital minute book, annual report or staff list names the residence, it would push the practice back nearly fifty years. Five of the nine were women, which in 1921 makes the house worth a note in its own right.

questions.title: Where did the Carr household live in 1921?
questions.detail: Three separate schedules were filed under 19 Park Terrace in the 1921 census: the Clark household (19 Park Terrace itself), the nine doctors at Broxtowe House, and Arthur Carr with his wife, a son of three, a visitor and three servants. The Carrs need a house. The enumerator's round puts them between Broxtowe House and Sunnyside. 20 Park Terrace is empty in the record for that year, and Sunnyside itself already holds two schedules.

questions.title: Which houses did the Weinberg and Smith families live in?
questions.detail: Twenty-two people were filed under 9 Cavendish Crescent North in the 1911 census, which is three schedules, not one household. Four servants with no head belong to Peveril House itself — Weston Fulford Marriott Weston-Webb held the lease and signed the return without being there on the night. The other two are the Weinbergs (nine people, head a shipping merchant and lace manufacturer) and the Smiths (nine people, head a lace manufacturer). The enumerator ran 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 up the crescent, and 10, 11 (Gleadthorpe) and 12 all hold no 1911 record, so the next two houses along are the candidates.

questions.title: Which house on Huntingdon Drive is Greendale? — answered: 4
questions.detail: Settled by A. Hagues: Joseph Spray's biography gives his address as Greendale, Huntingdon Drive, The Park, and Companies House records put Greendale at 4 Huntingdon Drive. The record already linked the Sprays to number 4 from 1911. 4 Huntingdon Drive now carries the name; press Record what you found to close this.

questions.title: Belwood is the corner of Tattershall Drive and Tennis Drive — which households were in it?
questions.detail: Found, or as near as makes no difference. A. Hagues has it on the street: a house at the Tattershall Drive corner with Tennis Drive carries BELWOOD on the post beside its door. The Land Registry postcodes agree — Belwood and Ellington are both NG7 1AD, along with the four flats at Tennis View, while Park Lodge and The Lodge sit apart in NG7 1BX. Ellington House (#312) is already in the record at that end of the street, so Belwood is its neighbour. What stands there now is modern: brick, flat-roofed, tall narrow windows, later 20th century by the look of it, so whatever Dougal de Havilland and the OS sheets recorded has gone and the name was carried over to its replacement. That is worth saying carefully — the name on a modern door is evidence of the site, not proof that the old house stood on the same footprint. What is still wanted is a household. No census entry anywhere in the record names Belwood, or any address on Tattershall Drive, so under this record's rule it stays a name rather than a property until somebody is found living in it. Dougal's map puts Belwood at x 174.0, y 403.3 with Hazelwood beside it at x 187.0, y 408.7 — the map's own coordinates, which nothing in the record can yet turn into a position on the ground.

questions.title: Penrhyn Cottage and Penrhyn House — one building or two?
questions.detail: The record holds Penrhyn House on Clumber Road East. Penrhyn Cottage turns up separately. Is the cottage the same building under an earlier or a smaller name, a lodge or coach house in its grounds, or a different building altogether? The Park has a number of coach houses turned into cottages and given their own name — Gartree Lodge is one — so a second building is entirely plausible.

questions.title: Gartree Lodge: standing, at 17a Tattershall Drive, and where the map puts it
questions.detail: Both halves answered on the ground by A. Hagues. It stands, it is 17a Tattershall Drive, and it goes by The Lodge now — which is why HM Land Registry's unnumbered "The Lodge" on this street is this house and not the lodge beside the tennis ground. And the position was right: he took the point this record already held, looked at it on Street View, and found the building exactly there. That point had been a calculated guess — the Tattershall Drive end of Gartree House's garden, 28m short of 4 Tattershall Drive along the line between them — so it is worth saying that the guess has been checked rather than merely left standing. The house began as part of the carriage and stable building at the bottom of Gartree House's garden, converted into a separate dwelling and addressed on the street the garden backs onto. In 1921 it held John Raven Erwin Hatton, a chauffeur of 28, and his wife Evelyn, 22 — a chauffeur housed over the stables of the house he drove for. Nothing here is open any longer; mark it answered on this page when you are ready, since an answer belongs to whoever made it rather than to the seed file.

questions.title: Is there a house at 14 Huntingdon Drive?
questions.detail: The 1921 census records Sidney Richard Tann, a chiropodist of 42, and his wife Daisy at "Huntingdon Drive (The Cottage)". The road is otherwise recorded only as far as number 10, so the number 14 is a guess and the house may no longer stand. Does anything of it survive, and where was it?

questions.title: Where exactly does The Hermitage stand?
questions.detail: Two positions are held for The Hermitage and they are 48 metres apart — one placed by hand, one derived. Nothing turns on it except the map, but on a site this small 48 metres is the difference between one building and its neighbour.

questions.title: What was Clumber Court?
questions.detail: Recorded as demolished, with no residents linked to it and no census year at all. Either the links have gone missing or the record was never more than a stub. What stood there, when did it go, and did anyone in the record live in it?

questions.title: Peveril House or Peveril Tower — which name, and when?
questions.detail: 9 Cavendish Crescent North is recorded under both names, and there is a second Peveril House on Peveril Drive. Which name did the Cavendish Crescent house carry, and over what period? The name clash is a live risk: a census address reading only "Peveril House" could be filed against either.

questions.title: What is the colour key on Dougal de Havilland's map?
questions.detail: The map colours the houses, and the colouring appears to encode the architect or the building period. Reading it off the scan gave forty suggestions that all fell into a single class, which is almost certainly wrong — the yellow road markings were being read as the yellow of one of the periods. Does a printed key exist, or does anyone remember what the colours meant? With the key, the map would name the architect of a great many houses at once.

questions.title: 171 names on Dougal's map have no house in the record
questions.detail: Mining the map turned up 964 labels. 86 matched a property outright; 171 are house-shaped names with nothing behind them. Some will be subdivisions and flats, some earlier names of houses already held, and some genuinely missing. Working the list down is the single largest source of new house names available, and most of it can be done from an armchair by anyone who knows the estate.

questions.title: Huntingdon Drive runs past number 10 — the record stops there
questions.detail: The record holds Huntingdon Drive as numbers 1 to 10. Dougal de Havilland's map draws a second run on the north-east side, numbered up the other way: 11 Burnham House, 13 The Magpies, 14 The Cottage, 15 The Coach House, The Hunting Lodge, 17, and 18 The Round House, formerly The Spiral, with Birchwood beyond. Only The Cottage is in the record, and only because a census household carried its name. Are these separate houses with their own numbers, or flats and coach houses belonging to houses already held? If they are houses, the record is missing half a street.

questions.title: Which of the two buildings by the tunnel is Gees Lodge?
questions.detail: Albert Drinkwater, a police constable, lived at "Gees Lodge, Tunnel Rd" in 1921 with his wife Ada and their son Harold. Two small buildings stand between Penrhyn House's garden and the road at the mouth of the Park Tunnel: the northern is still called Penrhyn Cottage, the southern is now called Tunnel Lodge. Gees Lodge is recorded on the southern one, since a lodge on Tunnel Road by the tunnel is the likelier of the two, but that is a judgement and not evidence. Is either still known by the older name? And is the reading Gees at all — the hand is loose enough that Cees or Lees are possible.

questions.title: Does anything of Barrack Yard survive, and exactly where was it?
questions.detail:
Three households were returned at "Barrack Yard, Barrack Lane" in 1911 — twelve people, all filed at 10 Barrack Lane because the enumerator counted the yard on the Barrack Lane round. Elizabeth Baker, a widow of 81, with her daughter and cabinet-maker son-in-law; Joseph Blythe, a sexton, with his wife, three children and a boarder; and Fletcher Hind, a domestic coachman, with his wife, a lace hand drawer, and their daughter, a hosiery machinist. A working court, in a lane otherwise recorded as eighteen numbered cottages.

It is now in the record as #410, placed at the foot of the lane just beyond number 30 and set back off the frontage. That position is worked out from Barrack Lane's own numbering and is provisional. Dougal de Havilland's map carries a note reading "Allegedly known as Barrack Yard" at the same end, around Pelham Cottages and Reveille, by the pedestrian access to Harlaxton Drive — allegedly is his word, and the map is far too coarse to place anything from.

Is the name still known? Does the entry or any of the cottages survive? And is the yard the block Dougal was pointing at, or somewhere else at that end of the lane?

questions.title: Is Yorke Mews its own address, or part of Yorke House?
questions.detail: A walk of the crescent turned up Yorke Mews, with the thought that it belongs to North Road rather than Cavendish Crescent North — made from an extension of the big house on the corner. The map agrees: Dougal de Havilland draws "Yorke Mews — The Lodge" and "formerly Yorke Cottage" immediately beside Yorke House, 6 North Road (#229), with The Coach House just beyond. So it is a mews of Yorke House. What is not known is whether it was ever a separate address with people returned at it, which is what it would take to give it a record of its own. Yorke Cottage is the older name and may be the one to search.

questions.title: 18 Cavendish Crescent North is still missing from the record
questions.detail:
The record held 16a and 18a but neither 16 nor 18 — although the listed-building descriptions of all four houses in that group name **"Nos. 16, 18, 20 and 22/24"** outright. They were built c.1885 as four substantial houses adjacent to each other, and three were later subdivided: the main part kept as one household, the former kitchen and butler's quarters made into a flat. So 16a is the flat of 16, and 18a the flat of 18.

**16 is now in the record as Crescent Lodge (#411)**, created because a census household was returned there. **18 still is not**, because nothing has yet been found living at it. What was 18 called, and is anyone on a return recorded there? And do 16 and 16a front the road differently, which would settle where each should sit on the map?

questions.title: 8 Cavendish Crescent North — the number survives on a door
questions.detail: The record runs 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 on the odd side and 10, 12, 14 upward on the even, with no 8 and no 6. A walk of the crescent found no house numbered 8, but **an old door with 8 on it at the back of the house below**. So the number was in use and the house has since been absorbed, renumbered or demolished. Which house does that door belong to now, and was 8 a separate dwelling?

questions.title: Western House School — sixty-three years, and two nights of it recorded
questions.detail:
**Where it was is settled.** The school stood at **30 The Ropewalk (#327)**, not 30 Western Terrace as first recorded. The 1891 census names it outright — schedule 195, "30 Ropewalk (Western House)" — with Louisa Clark, 59, Principal of a Private School, and three resident governesses.

By **1911** the house holds twenty people and is run by **Annie and Florence Green**, sisters from Beverley, both returned as Principal, with six teachers, four servants and eight boarding pupils. The 1911 return does not give the school a name, so whether it was still called Western House under the Greens is unknown.

What is open: who ran it between Louisa Clark and the Greens, and after them to 1937; whether the name changed; and what became of the building. Directories and prospectuses would answer all three. A curiosity worth chasing separately — three of the 1911 pupils are **Murchie** sisters, and two of them, Doris Mary and Phyllis Kathleen, were **born in Bangkok**, with the third born at Much Wenlock. A family abroad boarding its daughters in Nottingham.

questions.title: The Stables, Lenton Road — which house's stables?
questions.detail:
No census record in the record carries the address, so this comes from outside it. Two Lenton Road houses have a stables or coach house at the bottom of the garden, and both of those gardens back onto Clifton Terrace — the Gartree Lodge arrangement, where the outbuilding takes its address from the road behind.

**21 Lenton Road (#190)** is the stronger: its own listed description reads "Former coach house / stables building at bottom of garden facing Clifton Terrace now separately owned and converted for residential use" — separately owned is what gives a building its own address. **17 Lenton Road, Oakhyrst (#188)** has "Coach house and small outbuilding, now semi-derelict, added in garden area adjacent to Clifton Terrace c1900-1914". Cliff House (#196) has two flats in its converted coach house, but that is a 1959 conversion.

Dougal de Havilland's map carries three stables labels — "The Stables" beside The Chestnuts and 1 Kenilworth Road, and "The Stables 2a" with "Park Stables" over by Parkside and Lenton Avenue — but none of them on Lenton Road, so they are probably other buildings entirely.

Which house did it belong to, is it addressed on Lenton Road or Clifton Terrace, and was anyone ever returned as living there? 15, 17, 25 and 31 Lenton Road all hold people in 1911 and nobody at all in 1921, so there is room in the record for a household that has been filed somewhere else.

questions.title: Which building on Derby Road was the Bayley Hospital, and did any other Park house take wounded?
questions.detail:
**Settled: one did.** Claire Birkin (#65) turned her own house, **Newcastle Court, Newcastle Circus (#207)**, into an auxiliary hospital for officers during the First World War. She was awarded the Médaille de la Reconnaissance Française and the Médaille de la Reine Élisabeth of Belgium for that work, and she was also Commandant of the Radcliffe on Trent VAD, president of the Belgian Red Cross committee in Nottingham and chair of the American Red Cross Society. From the Birkin family account, by A. Hagues.

**Still open. Lilian Birkin** was Matron and Commandant of the **Bayley Hospital on Derby Road** from October 1914 — one of the first three auxiliary hospitals in England accepted by the War Office, taking the first Belgian wounded from Antwerp on 21 October 1914 and more than 1,600 casualties in four years. Derby Road is the northern boundary of this record, which holds numbers 117 to 173 and Rocky Mount. Which building was it, and is it one of ours? The name suggests the Bayleys, whose family the record holds at 9 Cavendish Crescent North.

Also unknown: how Lilian and Claire were related, and whether any house besides Newcastle Court took patients. The British Red Cross VAD records are searchable and would answer the last one.

questions.title: Which house on Cavendish Crescent North was called Kentmere?
questions.detail: In 1911 William Wing, a solicitor of 47, lived at "Kentmere, Cavendish Crescent North" with his wife Sara, sons Henry (an automobile engineer) and Richard (an articled clerk), a cook and a housemaid. The name is in the record under no house, and turns up on neither OpenStreetMap nor Dougal de Havilland's map. The enumerator reached the Wings straight after 4 Peveril Drive and before William Bradshaw and 3 Cavendish Crescent North, so Kentmere is at the North Road end of the crescent — most likely 1, now Carisbrooke House, which holds nobody in 1911. Names on this crescent changed: 10 was formerly Charnwood. A directory for about 1910, or a deed, would name it.

questions.title: Park Lodge is the last unplaced name on Tattershall Drive
questions.detail: Two of the three are settled. Belwood is the house at the corner with Tennis Drive, which carries the name on its door post and shares NG7 1AD with Ellington and the four flats at Tennis View; Ellington is Ellington House (#312), as expected. The Lodge is Gartree Lodge, 17a Tattershall Drive (#404), which is not what this question first guessed — it supposed The Lodge was the lodge beside the tennis ground that OpenStreetMap calls Park Lodge. That leaves Park Lodge itself, which the Land Registry holds separately at NG7 1BX alongside The Lodge, still unplaced. From HM Land Registry's price paid data, which records a house name beside the number for every sale since 1995. These are the names in use now, or recently — they may not be the historic ones, and a house name here is a lead, not a record. Under the rule for this record, none becomes a property until a census household is found at it, and Tattershall Drive holds no census household at all.

questions.title: Who ran Broadgate School after Ada Churley, and what happened to the houses in 1997?
questions.detail: Broadgate School occupied 1 and 2 Western Terrace from 1921 until 4 March 1997, initially run by Miss Ada Churley, who is on the 1921 census at number 1 as the principal of a school. Seventy-six years is longer than any household the record holds, and almost all of it is blank here: who ran the school after her, how many children it took, whether it used both houses from the start, and what became of the buildings after it closed. Both are flats now. Anyone who was taught there, or taught there, would settle most of this in an afternoon.

questions.title: Two girls' schools at 7 Western Terrace — when was each of them there?
questions.detail:
The house held Thornleigh Boarding and Day School for Girls, run by Miss E Leigh about 1900, and Auckland House School, a private boarding and day school for girls, briefly. Neither is dated here, and the record's only household at number 7 is the Hopewells in 1921 — a traveller of 65, his wife, a niece and two boarders — so neither school was there that year.

The 1901 return for the house should show Miss Leigh and her boarders outright, which would date Thornleigh and give the record a house full of women and girls that it does not have. Whether Auckland House came before or after is open, as is where each school went next. No Leigh is in the record at all.

Western Terrace held a third school in the same era: Broadgate took 1 and 2 from 1921 until 1997.

questions.title: Where is Claremont, and can the 1901 census place the Birkins in it?
questions.detail:
The Birkin family account puts Philip Austin Birkin at **Claremont** by the 1901 census. The record holds no house of that name, under any street or former name, and Philip appears in it only in 1911, at 5 Cavendish Crescent North — the house the account calls Blanbyre and the record holds as Blantyre House — where he is returned as a brewery manager.

So either Claremont is a Park house under a name this record does not yet know, or it stands outside the estate. The 1901 return that names it would settle both, and would be the evidence needed before any new property is created: nothing is added here without census data for it.

The same account places his brothers around him — Major Harry Birkin at Lincoln House on Lincoln Circus, Charles Wilfred at The Elms, now Newcastle Court, on Newcastle Circus, and Richard Lesley at Edale House on Clumber Road East. The record holds all three houses; Lincoln House has nobody in it at all.

questions.title: Lincoln Circus 1 and 2 — which houses are they? The record holds only two on the circus
questions.detail:
**Settled: number 3 is Lincoln House.** Harry Laurence Birkin's household of eight — him at 49, a lace manufacturer, his wife Olive and six servants — is now filed there, on the strength of the family account that puts Major Harry Birkin opposite his brother.

**Number 2 is open.** Edward Palmer and his wife Alice are returned there in 1921, he as a gardener of 57. Ten years earlier the same two were at **Gladstone House**, where he gave the same trade. So either Gladstone House is number 2 and they simply stayed put, or number 2 is a second dwelling on the same ground — a gardener's cottage or lodge — which would explain why Gladstone House's own 1921 household is a different set of people entirely: the Woodwards, Harriet Weselby, Kathleen Pollard and Annie Tune. A gardener living in the big house alongside another family is the less likely of the two.

**Number 1 is a house the record does not hold at all.** Six people in 1921: Alfred Charles Radford, 56, a lace and embroidery manufacturer, his wife Nellie, their daughter Doris, a trained nurse and two servants. Nothing on the circus in this record answers to it, so either a house is missing from the record or the numbering covers houses listed here under another street. A directory, or the 1911 return for the circus, would settle all of it.

questions.title: 1 Duke William Mount has no census household at all — where are the Fishers?
questions.detail:
The house was built c1878-80 for Horace Arthur Fisher, who moved in with his wife Sarah Kate after their first child was born in 1883, and they had six children. Not one census record in this record is filed there — 1891, 1901 and 1911 should each show the family in the house, and 1921 whoever followed them.

Eight Fishers are now in the record from the family account, with names but almost no dates. Any return for the house would date the children, give their occupations, and name the servants who are certainly missing. Note that Horace the son went by Frank, so a page may read Frank Fisher.

questions.title: Arundel House stood from 1870 — why is Stephen Wills not in any census for it?
questions.detail:
T. C. Hine built the house in 1870 for the lace manufacturer Stephen Wills, and the record's only household there is 1921: George Edward Dixon, steward of an institute, with his wife, two daughters and a niece. Searching the census for Wills at the address has come up empty, which is worth thinking about rather than simply repeating.

Things worth trying. The house may not have been **numbered** in the early returns — enumerators often wrote the name alone, so look for *Arundel House, Park Valley* rather than number 1, and for the corner given as Lenton Road, since the house stands on the junction. The record does hold early returns nearby — 15 and 25 Park Valley, and 23 Lenton Road, reach back to 1871 and beyond — so the pages themselves exist and the house should be on them.

It is also worth allowing that **he never lived here**. A manufacturer could commission a house to let, or build it for a son or a daughter. A trade directory for the 1870s would place Stephen Wills at whatever address he actually occupied, and if that is somewhere else, the account's "built for" means built to his order, not lived in by him. The 1871 return, taken within a year of completion, is the one to find first.
